method: search (discover) -> fetch (understand) -> grep (extract the quote); a quote may only come from a grep/fetch of the primary source; raw extracts in results/raw/

rows.claim_positioned: a contiguous mid-depth band decides refusal (the closest published statement to this run's positive)
rows.citation: Li, Yao, Zhang, Li, 2025, 'Safety Layers in Aligned Large Language Models: The Key to LLM Security', arXiv 2408.17003 (v5, 7 Apr 2025), ICLR 2025
rows.quote: identifying a small set of contiguous layers in the middle of the model that are crucial for distinguishing malicious queries from normal ones, referred to as "safety layers"
rows.establishes: Safety-critical parameters form a small CONTIGUOUS band in the middle of four aligned LLMs (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Llama-2-7b-chat, gemma-2b-it, Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct), located by layer-wise input-vector angle analysis, then refined by SCALING the parameters of candidate layer RANGES and reading an over-rejection count; SPPFT freezes those layers' gradients during fine-tuning.
rows.where_this_run_stops: This is the largest single narrowing of the positive. 2408.17003 already compares layer RANGES by editing their weights (scaling by alpha>1) and adjusting the range's upper and lower bounds. What it does not do: hold total removal energy and layer count fixed while moving the band; use a removal (orthogonalisation) edit rather than up-scaling; evaluate in any non-English language; or report an outside-family replication. The paper must cite it as prior work for 'contiguous middle layers matter' and claim only the matched-budget placement contrast.
rows.narrows: YES - strongly; the depth localisation and the range-comparison-by-weight-scaling are both prior work

rows.claim_positioned: prior work already varies a layer range's bounds and reads a behavioural metric
rows.citation: Li, Yao, Zhang, Li, 2025, arXiv 2408.17003, ICLR 2025
rows.quote: we evaluated the impact of different layer ranges on the security of aligned LLMs by scaling the parameter weights of the layers within the range
rows.establishes: The localisation procedure is itself a weight-space range comparison: scale layers i..j by alpha, count refusals on an over-rejection set, move the bound, keep the range that maximises the count.
rows.where_this_run_stops: The comparison is not energy-matched or count-matched (moving a bound changes both), the metric is over-rejection on benign prompts rather than residual harmful refusal, and the direction of the edit is amplification, not removal.
rows.narrows: YES - this is the sentence a reviewer would quote back

rows.claim_positioned: the uniform-spread-versus-norm-selected comparison this run must reconcile with
rows.citation: Hadetskyi et al., 2026, 'Not All Refusals Are Equal: How Safety Alignment Fails Cybersecurity at Scale', arXiv 2607.02714 (v2)
rows.quote: we opted for uniformly spread layer selection across 25–95% of model depth, which we found to [...] substantially outperform norm-based selection (targeting layers with the highest refusal signal norm) by up to ∼70pp of additional refusal reduction at 30%
rows.locator: Sec. 3.2 'Layer Selection Strategies' (PDF v2; identical in v1); detailed comparison in App. C [the quote spans a PDF page-break artifact; ' [...] ' marks where an interposed page number '4' sits in the extracted text]
rows.establishes: Across 24 models, spreading the selected layers over 25-95% of depth beats selecting the layers with the largest refusal-signal norm, by up to about 70 percentage points of additional refusal reduction.
rows.where_this_run_stops: This compares SELECTION CRITERIA (norm-ranked vs spread), not placements at matched energy and matched count; the figure is English-only and was not replicated here. Re-verified this session in the v2 PDF.
rows.narrows: PARTLY - it is a different comparison, which is why the reconciliation sentence is needed

rows.claim_positioned: adversarial search for a prior dose-versus-placement exchange result
rows.citation: searches 37, 38, 43 (this artifact's log); closest found: Bhandari and Wade, 2026, 'Steering Under Compression: Dose-Response, Capability Cost, and Failure Asymmetry in Quantized LLMs', arXiv 2609.06473
rows.quote: Using an iso-effect framework that compares capability costs at matched behavioral effect
rows.establishes: Matched-effect (iso-effect) comparison of activation steering under INT8/NF4 quantisation, with an explicit dose-response ladder and a collapse-floor pitfall; steering vectors stay collinear with FP16 siblings (cosine 0.945-0.998).
rows.where_this_run_stops: Activation steering, not weight edits; dose versus quantisation, not dose versus PLACEMENT; no language dimension. NO NEIGHBOUR FOUND for 'increasing the dose of a badly placed refusal edit does not substitute for moving it' - not found by these queries (rows 37, 38, 39, 43).
rows.narrows: NO - but it supplies the iso-effect vocabulary and the floor-anchoring warning this run's A1-A4 ladder hit

rows.claim_positioned: selecting WHERE to intervene by a discriminative criterion is established for activation steering
rows.citation: Dang and Ngo, 2026, 'Selective Steering: Norm-Preserving Control Through Discriminative Layer Selection', arXiv 2601.19375
rows.quote: discriminative layer selection that applies steering only where feature representations exhibit opposite-signed class alignment
rows.establishes: A layer-selection rule for activation steering over nine models, reporting 5.5x higher attack success than prior methods at ~100% capability retention.
rows.where_this_run_stops: Inference-time steering, English, no energy matching, no persistent weight edit.
rows.narrows: PARTLY - adds to the already-published 'where matters' line
